Overview


Most developer onboarding is still operationally weak.
A new engineer clones a repo, opens the README, installs dependencies, runs the obvious command, and still ends up blocked because the real setup path lives somewhere else.
Maybe CI is stricter than local. Maybe a service has to be running first. Maybe the package manager changed. Maybe generated files are required. Maybe the README test path is not the path that actually matters.
That is not just onboarding friction.
It means the repo never declared its onboarding truth clearly enough.
My view is simple: developer onboarding should be contract-first.
A repo should declare how onboarding actually works instead of asking every contributor to reconstruct it from prose, shell history, CI YAML, helper scripts, and maintainer fol…

articles.author: Jeferson Eiji
articles.description:
Handling database schema migrations in large systems presents unique challenges. Here’s how to approach this critical task effectively:
Version Control: Maintain migration scripts in version control alongside application code. This ensures consistency and traceability.


Automated Migrations: Use migration tools (e.g., Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic) to apply changes automatically and reliably across environments.


Backward Compatibility: Design migrations so that both old and new application versions can operate during rollouts. This often means creating additive changes first (e.g., adding new columns or tables) and delaying destructive changes (like column drops) until it’s safe.


Impact Analysis: Assess how migrations affect data integrity and system performance. For example, large table alterations can lock rows and affect uptime. Consider strategies such as batching or shadow tables.


Testing: Conduct thorough testing on database snapshots to catch issues before production deployment.




  
  
  Example: Column Addition


Suppose you want to add a last_login column to a users table:
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN last_login TIMESTAMP;

Deploy this migration.
Update application code to use the new column where required.
After verifying usage, you can remove any obsolete columns or fields.
Always include rollback scripts. For example:
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN last_login;

Be cautious—rollbacks might cause data loss if not properly managed.
For mission-critical systems, use advanced deployment strategies, such as:
Blue-green deployments for instant rollback.
Canary releases to test changes with a small user base first.
Phased migrations for massive datasets, updating data in smaller batches.
By adopting these practices, you can minimize risks and ensure smoother database schema transitions, even at scale.
articles.title: Best Practices for Database Schema Migrations in Large Systems

articles.author: Mirza Iqbal
articles.description:
If you have built a Model Context Protocol server with a passthrough tool, the kind that
I hit this building an open source MCP server for Hetzner. Listing worked perfectly. Every
A valid JSON document is required.

The body was arriving empty. Here is why, and the single line that fixed it.
First, here it is working. This server stands up a load-balanced stack and tears it back
  
  



  
  
  The symptom


A passthrough tool needs a free-form body so the model can send any payload. The obvious
body: z.unknown().optional()

Reads need no body, so every GET sailed through. The moment the model tried a POST, the
z.unknown() compiles to an empty JSON schema. Not an object, not a string, an empty shape.
Several MCP clients drop a property whose schema is empty. There is nothing to validate and
The cruel part is that the error comes from the upstream service, not from your server, so
Give the body a real schema. An object is enough, and accepting a JSON string as well makes
body: z.union([z.record(z.string(), z.unknown()), z.string()]).optional()

Then parse a string body into an object before you use it. The schema is now non-empty, so
A schema change you cannot see is a schema change you cannot trust. So I wrote a suite that
It caught the bug, proved the fix, and runs on every change now. The number that matters is
Two things to carry away.
Audit any tool that types an input as unknown or leaves it untyped. Give it a real schema.
Test write tools through the built server against the real service, not only your unit
tests. This failure only appeared at the client boundary.
The server I found this in is open source under MIT. It gives an AI assistant the full
npx -y hetzner-mcp

What is the most painful silent failure you have hit building MCP tools?
articles.title: Your MCP server's write tools are silently dropping their body
